More precise techniques include sticky routing, sending a user to the primary for a short window after they write; waiting for the replica to reach the log position of the write before reading, which some drivers support; and monitoring lag so you can stop routing to a replica that has fallen too far behind. Large transactions and bulk operations spike lag, so batching writes also helps keep replicas current.

whyImportant: Read replicas are a standard scaling tool, but using them naively introduces subtle, hard-to-reproduce consistency bugs that confuse users and corrupt workflows. Interviewers ask this to see whether you understand eventual consistency, can reason about which reads need freshness, and know practical patterns like read-your-writes routing rather than assuming replicas are interchangeable with the primary.
realWorldExample: After splitting reads to replicas, users reported that editing a comment and reloading showed the old text. The reload read from a replica that lagged by a couple of seconds behind the primary where the edit was written. We added read-your-writes routing so that for a few seconds after a user wrote, their reads went to the primary, while everyone else's browsing reads stayed on the replicas. The stale-edit reports stopped and the primary stayed offloaded.

nestedTopics.title: Read-your-own-writes consistency
nestedTopics.explanation: A consistency guarantee that a user always sees their own most recent write, even if others might briefly see stale data. It is typically implemented by routing a user's reads to the primary, or to a sufficiently caught-up replica, for a short window after they perform a write, preventing the confusing experience of a save that appears not to have taken effect.

nestedTopics.title: Causes of lag spikes
nestedTopics.explanation: Lag grows with heavy write volume, long single transactions that the replica must apply as one unit, replica hardware or I/O limits, and single-threaded apply on the replica. Bulk operations like large deletes or backfills are notorious for spiking lag, which is why batching big writes keeps replicas current and reads consistent.

nestedTopics.title: Routing reads by freshness requirement
nestedTopics.explanation: Not all reads need the latest data. Classifying reads by how much staleness they tolerate lets you send fresh-critical reads to the primary and staleness-tolerant reads to replicas, getting the read-scaling benefit of replicas without breaking the experiences that genuinely require up-to-the-moment data.

followUps.question: What is the read-your-own-writes problem and why is it so confusing for users?
followUps.answer: It happens when a user performs a write that goes to the primary, then immediately reads from a replica that has not yet caught up, so they see the data as it was before their change. To the user it looks like their save silently failed, even though it succeeded on the primary, so they often retry, creating duplicates, or report a bug that engineers cannot reproduce because by the time anyone checks, the replica has caught up. It is confusing precisely because it is transient and timing-dependent, and the fix is to guarantee a user sees at least their own latest writes by routing their reads appropriately.

followUps.question: How can you make a read wait for the replica to be current rather than always hitting the primary?
followUps.answer: When the write commits, the primary returns a log position or sequence number identifying that point in the replication stream. The application can remember this position for the user and, on a subsequent read, ask the replica whether it has applied up to at least that position, only reading from it once it has caught up, or briefly waiting until it does. Some database drivers and proxies support exactly this pattern. It gives read-your-writes consistency while still using the replica, rather than permanently sending the user to the primary, which keeps more read load off the primary while still guaranteeing freshness for that user.

followUps.question: How do you monitor and respond to excessive replication lag?
followUps.answer: I track the lag metric the engine exposes, such as the time or byte difference between the primary's current position and what the replica has applied, and alert when it crosses a threshold. When a replica lags too far, I take it out of the read rotation so the application stops serving very stale data from it, routing those reads to the primary or a healthier replica until it recovers. I also investigate the cause, which is often a large transaction, a bulk job, or replica resource saturation, and address it by batching the write or scaling the replica. The combination of monitoring, automatic removal of badly lagging replicas, and fixing the root cause keeps staleness within acceptable bounds.

question: How do you read an execution plan and turn it into a concrete fix?
directAnswer: I read the plan to find where the time and rows actually go, then translate that into a specific change. I look for the most expensive operator by cost or actual time, check for scans where a seek was possible, compare estimated against actual rows to spot bad statistics, and watch for expensive operators like sorts, spools, and key lookups. Each pattern maps to a fix: a scan plus a selective predicate means a missing index, a big estimate gap means update statistics, repeated key lookups mean add a covering index, and a sort means index in that order or reduce the rows sorted.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An execution plan is the optimizer's chosen recipe for running a query: the operators it will use, in what order, and its estimates for each. The actual plan adds real row counts and timings from running it. Reading it is interpreting that recipe to find the bottleneck.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: The optimizer translates declarative SQL into a concrete procedure, and the plan exposes that decision so humans can understand and influence performance. Without it you would be guessing why a query is slow; with it you can see exactly which step costs the most and why.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Read the plan by following data flow, typically right to left and bottom to top in graphical plans, and focus on actuals over estimates. First find the dominant operator, the one with the highest cost percentage or actual time. Then recognize patterns. A table or clustered index scan feeding a highly selective filter means the engine read everything and threw most away, pointing to a missing index on the filtered column. A large divergence between estimated and actual rows on an operator means the optimizer planned on bad information, so update statistics or address parameter sniffing. A key lookup repeated many times means the nonclustered index found the rows but had to fetch extra columns from the base table, fixed by a covering index that includes those columns. An expensive sort suggests providing an index already in that order or reducing the rows before sorting. Spools and large hash operations spilling to disk suggest reducing intermediate row volume. Each recognizable shape maps to a targeted change, and after applying it you re-capture the plan to confirm the operator and cost actually improved.

whyImportant: The execution plan is the single most direct evidence of why a query performs the way it does, and the ability to read it and translate patterns into fixes is the core skill of query tuning. Interviewers ask this because anyone can add a random index, but reading a plan shows you can diagnose precisely and fix the real bottleneck.
realWorldExample: A report query showed a nonclustered index seek followed by a key lookup executed two million times, which dominated the plan. The index found matching rows but had to jump back to the base table for three columns it did not contain. Adding those three columns as included columns made the index covering, the key lookup vanished from the plan, and the query went from twelve seconds to under one.

nestedTopics.title: Scan versus seek
nestedTopics.explanation: A seek navigates the index directly to the rows that match, reading only what it needs, while a scan reads the whole structure. A scan is correct when most rows match, but a scan combined with a selective filter signals a missing index, because the engine read everything just to keep a few rows.

nestedTopics.title: Key lookups and covering indexes
nestedTopics.explanation: When a nonclustered index lacks some columns a query needs, the engine does a key lookup back to the base table for each row, which is costly when repeated many times. Adding those columns to the index, as included columns, makes it covering, so the query is satisfied entirely from the index with no lookups.

nestedTopics.title: Estimate versus actual divergence
nestedTopics.explanation: Each operator shows estimated and actual rows. A big gap means the optimizer based its choices on wrong numbers, usually from stale statistics or parameter sniffing, leading it to pick join types and memory grants that do not fit reality. Spotting the gap tells you to fix statistics rather than the query shape.

followUps.question: What does a thick arrow between operators in a graphical plan tell you?
followUps.answer: Arrow thickness represents the number of rows flowing between operators, so a thick arrow means a large volume of rows is moving through that part of the plan. Thick arrows early in the plan that thin out later suggest the query reads many rows and filters them late, which is inefficient because you would rather filter early and carry fewer rows through joins and sorts. They draw your eye to where the heavy data movement happens, which is usually where the optimization opportunity is, for example pushing a filter earlier or adding an index so fewer rows enter the pipeline in the first place.

followUps.question: How do you know whether to add an index or update statistics from a plan?
followUps.answer: If the plan is doing a scan plus a selective filter, or a costly key lookup, the structure is the problem and an index is the fix: a new index for the scan, or a covering index for the lookup. If instead the plan shape looks reasonable but estimated and actual rows diverge wildly on operators, the optimizer made decisions on bad cardinality, so updating statistics, or addressing parameter sniffing, is the fix because it lets the optimizer choose correctly with the indexes it already has. In short, structural inefficiency points to indexing, while a good shape with bad estimates points to statistics.

followUps.question: Why focus on actual rows rather than estimated rows when tuning?
followUps.answer: Estimated rows are the optimizer's predictions and may be wrong, while actual rows are what really happened when the query ran, so they tell you the truth about where the work occurred. Tuning from estimates alone can mislead you, because the whole problem is often that the estimates were wrong. By looking at actuals you see which operators really processed the most rows and consumed the most time, and you also see the gap between estimate and actual, which itself is a diagnostic pointing at statistics problems. That is why you capture the actual execution plan, not just the estimated one, when tuning a real query.

question: How do you safely run a large backfill or data correction across millions of rows in production?
directAnswer: I run it in small, idempotent, resumable batches rather than one big statement. I size each batch to keep transactions short and locks brief, commit after each batch, and pause between batches to let other workloads and replication keep up. I make the operation idempotent so a re-run of a batch does no harm, track progress so I can resume after an interruption, run during low-traffic windows, and monitor lag, locks, and error rates throughout, ready to throttle or stop.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A backfill or large data correction is updating or populating a column across a huge number of existing rows, for example computing a new derived field or fixing bad data. Doing it safely in production means without long locks, log floods, replication lag, or risk of partial, unrepeatable damage.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Schema and business logic evolve, so existing data often needs to be migrated, corrected, or enriched. Because production tables are large and live, the correction cannot stop the world, and a single mistake across millions of rows is hard to undo, so the operation needs careful structure.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The foundation is batching by a stable key, usually the primary key, processing a bounded chunk like ten thousand rows per iteration, committing each batch, and pausing briefly between them. Short transactions keep locks brief and log generation steady so concurrent traffic and replicas keep up. The operation should be idempotent, meaning running a batch twice produces the same result, often achieved by updating only rows that still need it, for example a WHERE clause that excludes already-corrected rows, so a retry after a crash is safe. Progress is tracked, either implicitly by the key range processed or in a control table, so an interruption can resume rather than restart. You run during low-traffic windows, and you continuously monitor replication lag, lock waits, and the database's general health, throttling the batch rate or pausing if any of those degrade. For risky corrections you first run on a small sample or in a dry-run mode that reports what would change, and you keep the original values, via an audit table or backup, so the correction itself is reversible.

whyImportant: Backfills and corrections are routine in evolving systems but are exactly the operations that cause outages when done as one giant statement. Interviewers ask this to confirm you understand batching, idempotency, and resumability, and that you treat a mass data change as a controlled, monitored, reversible process rather than a single risky command.
realWorldExample: We needed to populate a new normalized region column derived from a messy address field across forty million customer rows. A single UPDATE would have locked the table and overwhelmed replication. We wrote a batched job that processed ten thousand rows per loop, updating only rows where the new column was still null so it was idempotent and resumable, paused fifty milliseconds between batches, and monitored replica lag. It ran over several hours overnight with no impact on the daytime application, and when the job crashed once we simply restarted it and it skipped the rows already done.

nestedTopics.title: Idempotency
nestedTopics.explanation: An idempotent operation produces the same result whether run once or many times. For a backfill this usually means each batch only touches rows not yet corrected, so re-running after a failure neither double-applies a change nor errors. Idempotency is what makes a long, interruptible job safe to retry.

nestedTopics.title: Resumability and progress tracking
nestedTopics.explanation: Because a long job may be interrupted, it must resume where it left off rather than restart. Driving batches by an increasing key range, or recording the last processed point, lets the job pick up after a crash without redoing finished work or skipping rows, which is essential for operations spanning hours.

nestedTopics.title: Throttling and monitoring
nestedTopics.explanation: A backfill competes with live traffic for resources, so you watch replication lag, lock waits, and load, and you dynamically slow down or pause if they degrade. Building in an adjustable pause between batches lets you dial the job's intensity up or down without restarting it, keeping production healthy.

followUps.question: How do you make a backfill idempotent in practice?
followUps.answer: The simplest way is to make each batch only affect rows that still need the change, by adding a predicate that excludes already-processed rows, for example WHERE new_column IS NULL when you are populating new_column, or a flag column you set as you go. That way if a batch is retried after a partial failure, the already-updated rows no longer match the predicate and are skipped, so the change is applied exactly once per row regardless of retries. The key is that the condition for needing the update becomes false once the update is done, which naturally prevents double application and makes the whole job safe to re-run.

followUps.question: How do you decide the batch size?
followUps.answer: Batch size trades throughput against impact. Too small and the job runs forever with high per-batch overhead; too large and each transaction holds locks longer, generates more log per commit, and spikes replication lag, defeating the purpose. I start with a moderate size like a few thousand to ten thousand rows, measure the per-batch duration, lock impact, and replica lag, and adjust: shrink it if lag or locking is a problem, grow it if the job is too slow and the system has headroom. The right size keeps each transaction short, on the order of well under a second, while making steady progress, and it depends on row width, indexes, and how busy the system is.

followUps.question: How do you make a risky data correction reversible?
followUps.answer: Before changing anything, I preserve the original values so I can restore them if the correction turns out to be wrong. That can mean copying the affected rows or just the original column values into a backup or audit table keyed by the row id, taking a table snapshot, or relying on point-in-time recovery. I also often do a dry run first that reports which rows would change and to what, so I can review the impact before committing real changes, and I may run the correction on a small sample and verify the results before unleashing it on all rows. Keeping the before-state and validating on a sample turns an irreversible mass change into one I can audit and roll back.

question: When and how do you update statistics, and why does it matter for production performance?
directAnswer: Statistics describe the distribution of data in columns and indexes, and the optimizer relies on them to estimate row counts and pick good plans. They go stale as data changes, leading to bad estimates and slow plans. I update them when I see large estimate-versus-actual gaps in plans, after big data loads or migrations, and on a schedule for large tables where the automatic threshold updates too rarely. I use sampled updates routinely and full scans for critical tables, and I treat updating statistics as the cheap first thing to try for many performance regressions.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Statistics are metadata the database keeps about how values are distributed in a column or index, such as the number of distinct values and a histogram of value frequencies. The optimizer uses them to predict how many rows each operation will touch.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: The optimizer is cost based, and cost depends on row counts. It cannot afford to count rows for every candidate plan, so it estimates from statistics. Accurate statistics produce accurate estimates and good plans; stale or missing statistics produce bad estimates and bad plans, so keeping them current is foundational to performance.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: When you query, the optimizer consults statistics to estimate selectivity, for example how many rows match a given filter, and chooses join types, join order, and memory grants accordingly. As inserts, updates, and deletes change the data, the stored distribution drifts from reality. Databases auto-update statistics after a proportion of rows change, but on very large tables that threshold can represent millions of rows, so statistics stay stale far too long between auto-updates. You update them manually with UPDATE STATISTICS or ANALYZE, choosing a sampling rate: a sample is fast and usually good enough, while a full scan is most accurate and worth it for important or skewed tables. The signal that statistics need attention is a plan where estimated rows diverge sharply from actual rows, which leads the optimizer to pick, say, a nested loop expecting a few rows when millions arrive. Because updating statistics is cheap relative to rebuilding indexes and often fixes regressions outright, it is usually the first low-risk remedy to try.

whyImportant: Stale statistics are behind a large share of sudden slowdowns, and updating them is one of the cheapest, safest fixes available, yet it is easy to overlook. Interviewers ask this to confirm you understand the optimizer is statistics-driven and that you reach for updating statistics, especially on big tables, before more expensive interventions.
realWorldExample: After a bulk import doubled a table's size, several queries slowed dramatically. The auto-update threshold had not yet triggered, so the optimizer still thought the table was half its real size and chose plans sized for the old volume. A simple UPDATE STATISTICS with a full scan on the affected table corrected the estimates and restored the plans immediately, far faster and safer than the index rebuild someone had proposed.

nestedTopics.title: Histograms and selectivity
nestedTopics.explanation: A histogram buckets a column's values and records how many rows fall in each range, letting the optimizer estimate how many rows a filter will match. Good histograms make selectivity estimates accurate, which is what lets the optimizer choose between a seek and a scan or pick the right join type.

nestedTopics.title: Sampling versus full scan
nestedTopics.explanation: Updating statistics by sampling reads only a fraction of rows, which is fast and usually accurate enough for evenly distributed data. A full scan reads every row for the most accurate distribution, important for skewed columns or critical tables where a sample might miss the skew and mislead the optimizer.

nestedTopics.title: Auto-update thresholds on large tables
nestedTopics.explanation: Engines auto-update statistics after a percentage of rows change, but on huge tables that percentage is an enormous absolute number, so statistics can stay stale for a long time. This is why large tables often need scheduled manual updates rather than relying on the automatic trigger.

followUps.question: What symptom in an execution plan tells you statistics are stale?
followUps.answer: The clearest sign is a large divergence between estimated rows and actual rows on plan operators. If an operator estimated ten rows but actually produced a million, the optimizer planned on data that no longer reflects reality, and you will often see it pick plan choices that fit the small estimate, like a nested loop or a tiny memory grant, that perform terribly against the real volume. That gap is the fingerprint of stale or missing statistics. When updating statistics closes the gap and the plan improves, it confirms the diagnosis. A plan with accurate estimates but still slow points elsewhere, like missing indexes.

followUps.question: Why might auto-update statistics not be enough on a large table?
followUps.answer: Auto-update fires after a certain fraction of rows have changed, and on a very large table that fraction translates to a huge number of modifications. So a table with hundreds of millions of rows might need tens of millions of changes before auto-update triggers, during which the statistics grow increasingly stale and the optimizer makes worse and worse decisions. Meanwhile a steady trickle of inserts that matters a lot for plan quality may never reach the threshold quickly. That is why large or fast-changing tables typically need a scheduled manual statistics update, often with a meaningful sample or full scan, rather than relying on the automatic mechanism alone.

followUps.question: Why is updating statistics often preferable to rebuilding an index for a regression?
followUps.answer: Because it is far cheaper and lower risk and frequently fixes the actual problem. An index rebuild generates large transaction log, consumes significant I/O and time, can block queries if done offline, and floods replicas, yet much of the benefit people attribute to a rebuild is really the statistics refresh it performs as a side effect. Updating statistics directly gets that benefit without the heavy structural operation. So for a regression that smells like bad estimates, updating statistics is the first thing to try: quick, safe, and often sufficient, reserving the expensive index rebuild for genuine fragmentation or density problems.

question: A stored procedure is intermittently slow with no code changes. How do you investigate?
directAnswer: Intermittent slowness with no code change almost always points to something environmental: parameter sniffing caching a bad plan, blocking from other sessions, stale statistics, or resource contention at certain times. I capture executions over time to find the pattern, check whether the slow runs correlate with specific parameters, plan changes, blocking, or a busy window, and inspect the cached plan and waits. The fix follows the cause: recompile or optimize-for to handle sniffing, tune blocking, refresh statistics, or address the resource contention.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Intermittent slowness is when the same code performs well most of the time but occasionally runs much slower, with no change to the procedure itself. The cause lies in conditions around the query rather than the query text.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A query's performance depends on more than its SQL: the cached plan, the parameter values, the freshness of statistics, what other sessions are doing, and available resources all vary over time. When these shift, the same code performs differently, producing intermittent rather than constant slowness.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The investigation is about finding the pattern behind the intermittency. First capture many executions with their duration, parameters, and plan, using Query Store or equivalent, and look for what the slow runs have in common. If slow runs cluster around particular parameter values or coincide with a plan change after a restart or statistics update, it is parameter sniffing: a plan compiled for one value misfits others. If slow runs coincide with high concurrency or specific times, it is likely blocking or resource contention, confirmed by checking waits and active sessions during those windows. If slowness grows gradually then resets, stale statistics that periodically auto-update may be the cause. Once the pattern names the cause, the remedy is targeted: OPTION (RECOMPILE) or OPTIMIZE FOR for sniffing, tuning the blockers or adjusting isolation for contention, scheduled statistics updates for staleness, or scaling and scheduling for resource pressure. The key is to gather evidence across time rather than judge from a single run, because a single fast run tells you nothing about why it is sometimes slow.

whyImportant: Intermittent problems are the hardest to debug because they are not reproducible on demand, and they erode trust because users hit them unpredictably. Interviewers ask this to see whether you can reason about the many time-varying factors around a query and gather evidence systematically, rather than declaring it fixed because it happened to run fast when you tested it.
realWorldExample: A pricing procedure was usually instant but slow for a few hours every so often. Query Store showed two plans for it, and the slow periods always followed a server restart that flushed the cache, after which the first call happened to be for a rare product with millions of price history rows, compiling a scan plan that then stuck for all normal lookups. Adding OPTION (RECOMPILE) let each call get an appropriate plan and the intermittent slowness vanished.

nestedTopics.title: Correlating slow runs with parameters
nestedTopics.explanation: By capturing the parameter values of each execution alongside its duration, you can see whether slow runs share particular values. If they do, the problem is data-skew-driven, often parameter sniffing, where one cached plan serves values with very different selectivity. The correlation is the evidence that points you at the cause.

nestedTopics.title: Time-of-day and concurrency patterns
nestedTopics.explanation: If slow runs cluster at certain times, the cause is likely external: peak concurrency causing blocking, a batch job competing for resources, or maintenance windows. Plotting slowness against time and load reveals contention that a single test run would never expose, redirecting you from the query to its environment.

nestedTopics.title: Plan history as evidence
nestedTopics.explanation: Query Store retains every plan a query has used with runtime stats, so you can see whether the procedure switched plans and when the slow periods align with a particular plan. This turns an intermittent mystery into a concrete observation: this plan is fast, that plan is slow, and here is when it switched.

followUps.question: How do you distinguish parameter sniffing from blocking as the cause of intermittent slowness?
followUps.answer: Parameter sniffing shows up as the same query running with different plans and the slow runs correlating with particular parameter values or with a recompile event like a restart or statistics update, and the query is slow even when nothing else is contending. Blocking shows up as lock wait time during the slow runs, with the slowness correlating to high concurrency or specific busy windows rather than to parameter values, and the cached plan being the same fast plan, just stuck waiting on locks. So I check the waits: if the slow runs are burning CPU or I/O executing a bad plan, it is sniffing; if they are sitting on lock waits, it is blocking. The evidence in the waits and the plan history tells them apart.

followUps.question: Why is capturing many executions more useful than profiling a single run?
followUps.answer: Because the problem is intermittent, a single run is likely to be a fast one, which tells you nothing about why it is sometimes slow, or it is a slow one without the context to know it is unusual. Only by capturing many executions over time, with their durations, parameters, plans, and the conditions around them, can you see the pattern that distinguishes the slow runs from the fast ones. That pattern, whether it is certain parameters, certain times, or a plan switch, is what reveals the cause. Debugging intermittent issues is fundamentally about gathering enough samples to separate signal from noise, which a one-off profile cannot do.

followUps.question: What if the slowness grows gradually and then suddenly resets?
followUps.answer: That sawtooth pattern strongly suggests statistics drifting stale and then being refreshed. As data changes, statistics grow out of date, estimates get progressively worse, and plans degrade, until an auto-update or a maintenance job refreshes the statistics and the optimizer suddenly gets good estimates again, resetting performance. The fix is to update statistics more frequently, on a schedule, so they never drift far enough to hurt, especially on large tables where the auto-update threshold is too high. Recognizing the gradual-degrade-then-reset shape is the clue that points specifically at statistics rather than sniffing or blocking.

question: How do you investigate a sudden spike in database CPU in production?
directAnswer: I find what is consuming the CPU rather than assuming. I look at the top queries by CPU using Query Store, pg_stat_statements, or the active sessions right now, and identify whether it is one runaway query, a query suddenly running with a worse plan, a spike in call volume, or missing indexes causing scans. I correlate the spike's start time with deploys, data growth, or stats changes. Then I target the specific offender: tune the query, fix the plan or statistics, add an index, or throttle the source of the call surge.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A CPU spike is a sudden, sustained rise in processor usage on the database server, which slows every query because they all compete for CPU. Investigating it means identifying which workload is responsible and why it changed.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: The database burns CPU executing query logic, sorting, hashing, and evaluating predicates. CPU spikes when queries do more work than before, either because more queries arrive, individual queries became more expensive due to plan or data changes, or inefficient queries are scanning instead of seeking. Pinpointing the cause is the whole task.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Start by ranking current and recent queries by total CPU, since CPU spikes usually trace to a small set of statements. Query Store and pg_stat_statements show top CPU consumers with call counts, which immediately distinguishes the two main causes. If one query's per-execution CPU jumped, suspect a plan regression or stale statistics making it scan or choose a bad join, and inspect its plan. If a query's call count exploded, the cause is upstream, a deploy, a retry storm, a cache failure pushing load onto the database, or a new feature, and the fix is in the application or rate limiting. Missing indexes cause scans that burn CPU comparing rows, visible as scans in plans. Correlate the spike's start with recent events: a deploy, a bulk load, a statistics change, or organic growth crossing a threshold. Once the offending query and reason are identified, apply the matching fix and confirm CPU drops. The discipline is evidence first: never tune blindly, because the wrong fix wastes the outage window.

whyImportant: CPU saturation degrades the entire database at once, so it is a common and urgent incident, and the instinct to throw hardware at it often masks a fixable query problem. Interviewers ask this to see whether you can quickly localize the cause to specific queries and distinguish a plan problem from a volume problem, which determines whether the fix is in the database or the application.
realWorldExample: CPU jumped to ninety percent right after a release. Top queries by CPU showed one lookup running ten times more often than before, because a caching layer the new code relied on was misconfigured and every request hit the database directly. The query itself was fine; the spike was pure call volume. Fixing the cache configuration dropped CPU back to normal, whereas tuning the query would have wasted time on a non-problem.

nestedTopics.title: Per-execution cost versus call volume
nestedTopics.explanation: Total CPU equals cost per call times number of calls, so a spike is either calls getting more expensive or more calls arriving. Distinguishing these is the first fork: expensive calls mean a plan or index problem in the database, while a call surge means an application or upstream cause. Looking at call counts alongside CPU answers it immediately.

nestedTopics.title: Scans burning CPU
nestedTopics.explanation: A query lacking a suitable index scans large amounts of data, evaluating the predicate against every row, which consumes CPU as well as I/O. When several such queries run, CPU climbs. Spotting scans in the top consumers' plans points to missing indexes as a CPU fix, not just an I/O one.

nestedTopics.title: Correlating with recent events
nestedTopics.explanation: Spikes rarely happen for no reason, so aligning the start time with deploys, data loads, statistics updates, or organic growth narrows the cause fast. A spike that begins exactly at a release time implicates the release; one that grows gradually implicates data volume crossing a threshold.

followUps.question: How do you tell whether a CPU spike is from one query or many?
followUps.answer: I rank queries by total CPU consumed over the spike window using Query Store or pg_stat_statements. If a single query or a couple dominate the total, the spike is concentrated and I focus there. If CPU is spread across many queries with none dominating, the cause is more systemic, like a general load increase, a resource shortage forcing more physical work, or an instance-wide issue such as statistics being flushed. The shape of the top-consumers list tells me whether to chase one offender or look for a broader cause, which completely changes the investigation path.

followUps.question: Why might adding hardware be the wrong first response to a CPU spike?
followUps.answer: Because most CPU spikes are caused by a specific fixable problem, a bad plan, a missing index, or a surge of unnecessary calls, and adding CPU only masks it temporarily while the underlying inefficiency keeps growing. You pay for more hardware and the problem returns as load increases further. Worse, if the spike is a call-volume bug like a retry storm or a broken cache, more hardware does nothing to address the real issue in the application. The right first move is to identify the offending query and reason, because a single index or query fix often eliminates the spike entirely at no cost, and only genuine sustained growth justifies more hardware.

followUps.question: What application-side causes can show up as a database CPU spike?
followUps.answer: Plenty, because the database executes whatever the application sends. A deploy that introduces an inefficient query or removes a needed index, a caching layer that fails or is misconfigured so every request hits the database, a retry storm where failing requests hammer the database repeatedly, an N+1 query pattern firing many small queries per request, or a new feature with unexpectedly high traffic. In all of these the database is healthy and simply doing more work because of the application. That is why I always check whether the spike is per-execution cost or call volume, since a volume spike sends me to the application rather than to query tuning.

question: How do you handle a deadlock that is recurring in production?
directAnswer: A deadlock is a cycle where two transactions each hold a lock the other needs, so the engine kills one as the victim. For a recurring deadlock I first capture the deadlock graph, which shows the two statements, the resources, and the lock order involved. The most common root cause is transactions acquiring locks in different orders, so the primary fix is to make all code access tables and rows in a consistent order. I also shorten transactions, add indexes to reduce the locked footprint, and ensure the application retries the victim, since deadlocks can never be fully eliminated.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A deadlock is a mutual blocking cycle: transaction A holds a lock B wants while B holds a lock A wants, so neither can proceed. The database detects the cycle and aborts one transaction, the victim, to let the other continue. A recurring deadlock is this happening repeatedly under normal operation.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Deadlocks arise naturally from concurrency plus locking when transactions acquire multiple locks in conflicting orders. They are not a bug in the database; they are an inherent possibility whenever concurrent transactions touch overlapping resources in inconsistent sequences. The engine resolves them automatically by sacrificing a victim, but recurring ones signal a design issue worth fixing.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Begin with evidence: capture the deadlock graph, which most engines can log, showing the participating statements, the locks each held and requested, and the resources at the center of the cycle. The classic pattern is inconsistent lock ordering: one code path updates table X then table Y, another updates Y then X, and under concurrency they can deadlock. The primary remedy is to enforce a consistent access order everywhere so cycles cannot form. Other contributors include long transactions that hold locks longer, giving more chance to collide, and missing indexes that force scans locking many rows, widening the conflict surface, so shortening transactions and adding indexes both reduce deadlock frequency. Lower isolation levels or snapshot isolation can avoid some reader-writer deadlocks. Crucially, because you can reduce but never guarantee zero deadlocks, the application must catch the deadlock victim error and retry the transaction, which makes deadlocks a recoverable, transient event rather than a user-facing failure. So the full answer is: capture the graph, fix the ordering and footprint, and ensure retry.

whyImportant: Recurring deadlocks cause failed transactions and user errors, and they are a clear signal of a concurrency design flaw. Interviewers ask this to test deep understanding of locking and transactions, the ability to read a deadlock graph, and the mature recognition that deadlocks must be both reduced through design and handled through retry, not just wished away.
realWorldExample: Two services updated an accounts table and a ledger table but in opposite orders, and under load they deadlocked dozens of times an hour, failing transfers. The deadlock graph made the opposing lock order obvious. We standardized both code paths to update accounts before ledger, which removed the cycle, and added a retry around the transaction as a backstop. Deadlocks dropped to essentially zero and the rare survivor was retried transparently.

nestedTopics.title: The deadlock graph
nestedTopics.explanation: The deadlock graph is the engine's record of a deadlock, naming the two transactions, the statements each was running, the locks held and requested, and the chosen victim. It is the single best piece of evidence because it shows exactly which resources and in which order created the cycle, pointing directly at the inconsistent ordering to fix.

nestedTopics.title: Consistent lock ordering
nestedTopics.explanation: If every transaction always acquires locks on shared resources in the same order, a cycle cannot form, because no two transactions can each be holding what the other wants next. Standardizing access order across the codebase, for example always touching parent before child or tables alphabetically, is the most reliable structural deadlock fix.

nestedTopics.title: Retry of the victim
nestedTopics.explanation: Because deadlocks cannot be fully prevented, robust applications catch the deadlock-victim error and simply retry the aborted transaction, often after a tiny backoff. Since the conflicting transaction has by then completed, the retry usually succeeds, turning deadlocks into an invisible, self-healing event rather than a user-facing error.

followUps.question: How does the database decide which transaction becomes the deadlock victim?
followUps.answer: The engine generally picks the transaction that is cheapest to roll back, typically the one that has done the least work, measured by how much log it has generated, so that aborting and undoing it costs the least. Some engines let you influence this with a deadlock priority setting, so you can mark a critical transaction as less likely to be chosen as the victim. The victim's transaction is rolled back entirely and it receives a specific deadlock error, while the other transaction proceeds normally. Understanding this helps you design which transactions should retry and which you might prioritize to survive.

followUps.question: Why can adding an index reduce deadlocks?
followUps.answer: Without a suitable index, a statement that filters or updates rows must scan, which takes locks on many more rows or pages than the few it actually cares about, widening the surface where it can conflict with other transactions. A precise index lets the statement seek directly to and lock only the rows it needs, shrinking its locked footprint and the window during which it holds those locks. Smaller, briefer locks mean fewer overlaps with concurrent transactions, so the chance of forming a deadlock cycle drops. Thus indexing is not only a performance fix but also a concurrency fix that reduces both blocking and deadlocks.

followUps.question: If deadlocks cannot be eliminated entirely, what is the right overall strategy?
followUps.answer: A two-pronged approach: reduce their frequency through design, and handle the residue through retry. On the design side, enforce consistent lock ordering, keep transactions short, add indexes to shrink the locked footprint, and use appropriate isolation levels, which together make deadlocks rare. On the handling side, wrap transactions in retry logic that catches the deadlock-victim error and re-runs the transaction, usually succeeding on the second attempt because the conflict has cleared. This acknowledges that under concurrency a residual deadlock rate is inevitable, so the goal is to make them rare enough not to matter and harmless when they do occur, rather than chasing an impossible zero.
